theory.intro: Many 3D lengths are found by spotting a right-angled triangle inside the solid. A face diagonal crosses one face and is the hypotenuse of a triangle whose two shorter sides are edges of that face. The slant height of a cone, and the longest rod across a cylinder, work the same way. Keep a surd exact unless the question asks you to round.
facts: A **face diagonal** crosses a single face; it is the **hypotenuse** of a right-angled triangle whose two shorter sides are **edges** of that face.
To find a face diagonal, add the squares of the two edges: $d=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$.
The **slant height** of a cone is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with shorter sides the **radius** and the **perpendicular height**: $s=\sqrt{r^{2}+h^{2}}$.
To find a shorter side instead of the hypotenuse, subtract: $a=\sqrt{d^{2}-b^{2}}$.
Leave a surd such as $\sqrt{61}$ for an exact answer; round only when the question asks.
steps: Identify the right-angled triangle and its two known sides.
Decide whether the unknown is the hypotenuse or a shorter side.
Apply Pythagoras' theorem and round only if required.

mastery.solution_text:
Front face (width $6$, height $9$): $\sqrt{6^{2}+9^{2}}=\sqrt{117}\text{ cm}$
Side face (depth $4$, height $9$): $\sqrt{4^{2}+9^{2}}=\sqrt{97}\text{ cm}$
Top face (depth $4$, width $6$): $\sqrt{4^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{52}\text{ cm}$
The front face has the longest diagonal, $\sqrt{117}\text{ cm}$.

First find the width $AB$ from the front face, where $AF$ is the hypotenuse.
$AB=\sqrt{13^{2}-5^{2}}$
$=\sqrt{144}$
$=12\text{ cm}$
Now $EG$ is the top face diagonal, with shorter sides the width $12\text{ cm}$ and the depth $9\text{ cm}$.
$EG=\sqrt{12^{2}+9^{2}}$
$=\sqrt{225}$
$=15\text{ cm}$
